question: Why does this useEffect stale closure bug log old count? const [count, setCount] = useState(0); useEffect(() => { setTimeout(() => { console.log(count); }, 1000); }, []);
options: Dependency array [] captures count once; timeout logs 0 forever
count updates before timeout fires
Dependencies are ignored in this case
useEffect doesn't create closures
explanation: Empty dependency array [] means the effect (and its closure over count) runs once; count stays 0 in the closure while the real count increments.

question: Given useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(fn, 1000); }, []), why is the interval never cleared on unmount?
options: No cleanup function returned; interval persists after unmount
useEffect auto-clears intervals
Return statement is not needed
Intervals are always cleaned up
explanation: useEffect must return a cleanup function to clear intervals/timers/subscriptions; without it, the interval runs forever even after the component unmounts.

question: Why might useCallback(fn, [x]) cause a child component to re-render even though the callback dependency didn't change? const fn = useCallback(() => console.log(y), [x]);
options: y is stale in the callback, but x changing causes new reference
useCallback prevents all re-renders
y should be in dependencies, causing unnecessary new reference
This pattern has no re-render issues
explanation: y is used but not in dependencies; when y changes, useCallback doesn't know and doesn't create a new reference, so stale y is passed to child.

question: Given useMemo(() => { return obj; }, [obj]), when does the memoized value update and why?
options: Only when obj reference changes (shallow compare deps), even if obj.x changes
Every render, useMemo doesn't actually memoize
Only when useMemo dependency array is empty
useMemo always creates new values
explanation: useMemo compares dependencies with ===; obj reference matters, not contents, so obj.x change doesn't trigger recompute unless obj itself is new.

question: Why might useRef(null) in a child prevent the parent from getting the DOM ref? const ref = useRef(null);
options: useRef doesn't forward refs automatically; parent needs forwardRef to access
useRef exports refs automatically
refs are always accessible to parents
forwardRef is not related to useRef
explanation: useRef creates a ref on the child component itself; the parent cannot access it unless the child explicitly forwards with React.forwardRef().

question: Given useEffect(() => fetch(url), [url]), why might skipping this dependency cause stale data?
options: Omitting url means fetch runs once at mount, url changes don't re-fetch
Dependencies are optional, effect runs every render anyway
Fetch is cached automatically
useEffect must have at least one dependency
explanation: Without url in dependencies, the effect runs once; if url changes, the old fetch URL is cached, and new data is never fetched.

question: Why does useCallback(() => setX(x + 1), []) create a stale-closure bug? const [x, setX] = useState(0);
options: Empty deps capture x=0; callbacks always increment by 1 even after multiple renders
useCallback auto-updates dependencies
x is not needed in dependencies
This pattern has no stale-closure issues
explanation: [] captures the closure with x=0 forever; setX(x + 1) always evaluates to setX(1), not the current value; use setX(prev => prev + 1) instead.

question: Given useLayoutEffect vs useEffect, why might useLayoutEffect block paint? useLayoutEffect(() => { ... }, []);
options: useLayoutEffect runs synchronously before browser paint, useEffect after
Both run asynchronously
useLayoutEffect is faster
Paint always happens before both hooks
explanation: useLayoutEffect blocks paint; if it's slow, the screen freezes; useEffect is safer for most cases, runs after paint and doesn't block visuals.

question: Why might useContext cause unnecessary re-renders when the context value is a new object? const value = { x: 1 }; return <Context.Provider value={value}>;
options: New object on every render triggers all consumers to re-render
Context caches values, no re-renders
Object identity doesn't matter for context
useContext never re-renders
explanation: Context uses === to detect changes; { x: 1 } is a new object every render, so all consumers re-render even if x didn't change.

question: Given useReducer, why might it be preferred over useState for complex state logic? const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initial);
options: Reducer centralizes logic, handles multiple updates predictably
useState is simpler and always better
useReducer is slower than useState
Complex logic cannot be handled by either
explanation: useReducer groups related state updates into actions, making complex state transformations more predictable and testable than multiple setStates.
